newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czech premier Klaus battles arrogant reputation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czech premier Klaus battles arrogant reputation.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, sometimes called Margaret Thatcher's man in the East, shares at least one trait with the former British leader: he is arrogant, or so his enemies and some allies say.
Like Thatcher, he proclaims his devotion to the free market, his criticism of European Union bureaucracy and his determination to push on with reform against all odds.
Also like Thatcher, who as prime minister from 1979 to 1990 sometimes reduced cabinet colleagues to tears, Klaus has never lost a parliamentary election.

But while Thatcher's three general election victories as Conservative leader were convincing, the 55-year-old Czech economics professor flirted with defeat in lower house polls last June when his government lost its majority.

Weakened and harried by his arch-rival, Social Democrat chairman Milos Zeman, Klaus now has to win Senate elections starting this weekend well if he is to have any hope of matching Thatcher's record of 11 years in power.

Klaus, a member of the lower house, is not running for the Senate which has few powers. But he has featured in campaigning for his centre-right Civic Democratic Party (ODS) and the November 15-16 polls will give Czechs the first chance to vote on his record since the inconclusive lower house elections.
It will be a tight race. Most opinion polls show ODS has lost the lead it held over the Social Democrats in June.
Elections are fought over policies but also over personalities. This may be Klaus's weakness in the Senate race.
Analysts have long hailed Klaus for the remarkable economic transition from communism he led first as Czechoslovak Finance Minister from 1989 to 1992 and since then as Czech premier.
So dominant, or perhaps domineering, is Klaus's personality that it has become a lively topic of conversation from ambassadorial dinner tables to the local beer hall.
Klaus's opponents make the most of it. Zeman, a personal enemy long before the 1989 fall of communism, directs his message against the party Klaus chairs but the target is clear.

"The arrogant stance of ODS...has led to the situation where a critical mood is growing significantly among Social Democrats," Zeman said. "A willingness to tolerate, or even suppport, the minority government is declining significantly."

The little-reformed communists accuse Klaus of the same thing despite his weaker position. "If Vaclav Klaus feels unfavourable restrictions by parliament, he is only proving his arrogance and unwillingness to submit to the principles of parliamentary democracy," said spokeswoman Vera Zezulkova.

Similar accusations also come from political allies, albeit in coded form. Last year Jan Kalvoda, who leads a junior partner in Klaus's three-party coalition, attacked "arrogant Czech Euroscepticism (which is) allegedly eurorealism".
Klaus has frequently criticised the European Union for bureaucratic tendencies even though he lodged the Czech Republic's application to join early this year.

Even Klaus supporters admit that he is a difficult man to work with, although they accept this because of his record of achieving steady economic growth, almost negligible unemployment and cutting inflation to single figures.
A former aide says that, as a professor, he likes lecturing people. But Klaus, an unorthodox economist under communism, rejects suggestions that he tries to run a one-man show.

"Various cliches have been created about me. Some of my colleagues laugh and tell me: 'prime minister, you should finally start being arrogant so that people know what being arrogant is like' ... I think it is quite a good idea," he said in a recent radio interview.

"It is far from true that I win every time ... If I am outvoted in a cabinet meeting, I go to a news conference without batting an eyelid and say that the cabinet has decided on this or that," he said. "I do not add that I had a different, much better and much more clever view."
Whether Klaus's perceived arrogance will cost ODS many votes in the Senate elections remains to be seen.
Some opinion polls after the June elections indicated some voters did desert ODS due to Klaus, usually to one of his two conservative coalition partners rather than the opposition.

The first past the post system used in the Senate elections may benefit Klaus. Candidates must win over half the vote and the fight in most, if not all, 81 constituencies is expected to go to a second round run-off on November 22-23.
These are likely to be mostly showdowns between the two biggest parties, the ODS and Social Democrats, meaning conservative voters have little choice but to back Klaus.

Again like Thatcher, Klaus may find an unexpected ally in an opposition which is divided or has weak leadership. The Social Democrats are split over whether to back the 1997 state budget and bickering over the communist pasts of some members.
Showing he has lost few of his political skills, Klaus has leapt on Zeman's embarrassment. He is also ready to knock back any attacks from "friends" as well as foes.

"It is sad that some criticism also comes from the government coalition camp," he said. "It is only further proof of how easily people who do not bear the main share of responsibility can pronouce such showy statements."
